title: 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design (Jakob Nielsen, 1994, updated 30 January 2024)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. The ten heuristics by name; first developed with Rolf Molich in 1990, published by Nielsen in 1994; page updated 30 January 2024.

title: Severity Ratings for Usability Problems (Jakob Nielsen, 1 November 1994)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Severity combines frequency, impact and persistence, plus market impact; the 0 to 4 scale from not a problem to usability catastrophe.

title: Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users (Jakob Nielsen, 18 March 2000)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Five users find about 85% of problems under a model where one user finds about 31%; run several small rounds; 3 to 4 users per group for two distinct groups; about 20 users for quantitative studies and about 15 for card sorting.

title: Thinking Aloud: The #1 Usability Tool (Jakob Nielsen, 15 January 2012)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. How a think-aloud test works, its low cost and flexibility, and its limits: no detailed statistics, unnatural for users, facilitator prompts can bias behaviour.

title: Card Sorting: Uncover Users' Mental Models (Samhita Tankala and Katie Sherwin, 2 February 2024)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Open, closed and hybrid card sorts; at least 15 participants for qualitative and 30 to 50 for quantitative sorts; 30 to 50 cards; moderated versus unmoderated.

title: Tree Testing: Fast, Iterative Evaluation of Menu Labels and Categories (Page Laubheimer, 6 August 2023, reviewed 19 August 2026)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Tree testing evaluates a text-only hierarchy; card sorting generates it; success, directness and time on task; task wording that does not give away the answer; a warm-up task.

title: Error-Message Guidelines (Tim Neusesser and Evan Sunwall, 14 May 2023)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Place errors near the problem, never by colour alone, plain language, specific cause, constructive fix, no blame or humour, keep the user's input.

title: Synthetic Users: If, When, and How to Use AI-Generated Research (Maria Rosala and Kate Moran, 21 June 2024)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. AI-generated users are useful for desk research, piloting guides and hypotheses; they idealise behaviour, give shallow insight and cannot validate concepts; supplement, never replace, real research.

title: Don't Make Me Think, Revisited (Steve Krug, third edition, 2014)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. The third edition (New Riders, 2014) and the author's aim: usability work is valuable and much of it is not hard; principles extended to apps and other things people use.

title: Measuring Usability with the System Usability Scale (SUS) (Jeff Sauro, 3 February 2011)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. SUS created by John Brooke in 1986; 10 items; scoring to 0 to 100; average about 68 across about 500 studies; scores are percentiles, not percentages; use confidence intervals with small samples.

title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (dated version 12 December 2024)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Current dated Recommendation 12 December 2024; contrast 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for large text (1.4.3); reflow at 320 CSS pixels wide (1.4.10); Focus Not Obscured (Minimum).

title: What's New in WCAG 2.2
supports: Opened with WebFetch. WCAG 2.2 became a Recommendation on 5 October 2023; the nine new success criteria and their levels; 4.1.1 Parsing removed as obsolete.

title: Understanding Success Criterion 2.5.8: Target Size (Minimum) (updated 2 November 2026)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Pointer targets at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, with five exceptions: spacing, equivalent, inline, user agent control, essential.

title: Understanding Success Criterion 3.3.8: Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (updated 6 September 2026)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. No cognitive function test such as remembering a password or solving a puzzle at sign-in unless there is an alternative, a mechanism such as a password manager or paste, object recognition, or personal content.

title: Easy Checks: A First Review of Web Accessibility (updated 9 August 2023)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Ten quick checks (page title, alt text, headings, contrast, resize text, keyboard and focus, forms and errors, moving content, multimedia, structure); a page can pass them and still have barriers; judging alt text needs a person.

title: The WebAIM Million: 2026 report on the accessibility of the top 1,000,000 home pages (updated 30 March 2026)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. February 2026 data: 95.9% of home pages had detected WCAG 2 failures, 56.1 errors per page; most common failures and their shares.

title: Guidance on Web Accessibility and the ADA (18 March 2022)
publisher: US Department of Justice, Civil Rights Division (ADA.gov)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. The ADA applies to web offerings of businesses open to the public and of state and local governments; no regulation sets detailed technical standards for businesses; WCAG and Section 508 named as helpful guidance; banner noting the separate 2024 rule for governments.

title: Fact Sheet: New Rule on the Accessibility of Web Content and Mobile Apps Provided by State and Local Governments
publisher: US Department of Justice, Civil Rights Division (ADA.gov)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Title II rule sets WCAG 2.1 Level AA; an Interim Final Rule of 20 April 2026 moved compliance to 26 April 2027 (50,000 people or more) and 26 April 2028 (smaller entities and special districts).

title: A new era for inclusion begins: the European Accessibility Act enters into force (27 June 2025)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. European Accessibility Act requirements apply from 28 June 2025 and cover e-commerce, online banking, transport websites and apps, e-books, computers and smartphones, among others.

title: Understanding accessibility requirements for public sector bodies (updated 30 September 2024)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. UK public sector websites and apps must meet WCAG 2.2 AA and publish an accessibility statement; all UK service providers must make reasonable adjustments under the Equality Act 2010 (Disability Discrimination Act 1995 in Northern Ireland).

title: Using moderated usability testing (updated 3 October 2017)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Recruit actual or likely users; realistic tasks that do not hint at the answer; a discussion guide; a note-taker per session; no more than six one-hour sessions a day with at least 15 minutes between them.

title: Writing for user interfaces (updated 16 April 2018)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Use users' own words, start with less content, front-load key words, link text that makes sense alone, no meaning by colour or position, sorry only when something serious has gone wrong, aim to be boring.

title: Error message (component guidance)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Show the error next to the question and in an error summary with the same words; say what happened and how to fix it; avoid blame words, please, sorry, valid or invalid, and oops; keep entered answers (change listed January 2024).

title: UI Design Dos and Don'ts
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Controls at least 44 by 44 points so they can be tapped accurately; text at least 11 points; ample contrast.

title: Make apps more accessible
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Touch targets of at least 48 by 48 dp; text contrast of 4.5:1 below 18sp (or 14sp bold), 3:1 otherwise; describe each control's purpose, not its look.

title: The Digital Services Act (page updated 1 October 2026)
publisher: European Commission, Shaping Europe's digital future
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Lists a ban on dark patterns: deceptive design such as aggressive pop-ups or confusing and misleading consent buttons is prohibited for online platforms.

title: Review of EU consumer law (Digital Fairness Act and fitness check)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. The Digital Fairness Act is under preparation and aims at dark patterns, addictive design, unfair personalisation, influencer marketing, price marketing and digital contracts; the fitness check report was published in October 2024.

title: FTC Report Shows Rise in Sophisticated Dark Patterns Designed to Trick and Trap Consumers (15 September 2022)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. The four dark pattern tactics in the FTC staff report: disguising ads, making cancellation hard, burying key terms and junk fees, tricking people into sharing data.

title: Cart Abandonment Rate Statistics (updated 28 October 2026)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Average documented cart abandonment 70.22% across 50 studies (2006 to 2025); checkout abandonment reasons among US shoppers, including extra costs 40%, forced account creation 18% and a long or complicated checkout 17%; sample size and year not shown on the page.

title: Guide to the Figma MCP server
supports: Opened with WebFetch (no page date shown). Remote server recommended; agents can read design context and, in beta, write frames, components and variables to the canvas; writing outside your drafts needs a Full seat; canvas writing free during beta, later usage-based.
